WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- Secretary of State Hillary Clinton reached an important milestone Wednesday in her quest to pay the debt from her failed 2008 presidential bid: For the first time in eight months, her campaign committee reported having more money in the bank than it owes. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's campaign committee reported owing $2.3 million in debt at the end of March. On a day most Americans were preoccupied with filing their federal income taxes, Clinton's campaign committee filed finance documents with the Federal Election Commission, reporting a total of $2.3 million in debts at the end of March, compared with $2.6 million in the bank. The nation's top diplomat has been steadily chipping away at unpaid campaign bills since suspending her White House bid in June 2008, when her debt peaked at $25.2 million. That amount covered $12 million owed to vendors, as well as the $13.2 million she loaned her campaign from personal funds. Clinton's campaign was unable to repay that personal loan by the time the Democratic National Convention convened in Denver, Colorado, last August, the deadline mandated by the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. The former New York senator was forced to forgive the entire loan amount. Her campaign owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors at the end of November; $5.9 million to five creditors at the end of December; and the current $2.3 million owed to just one creditor at the end of March. That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential bid. The firm's president, Mark Penn, was Clinton's senior campaign strategist until he stepped down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia for a U.S.-Colombia trade deal that Clinton opposed. Penn remained involved with the campaign. Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters raced to pay as much of the debt as possible by the time she was confirmed and sworn in as the nation's 67th secretary of state on January 21. As of that date, Clinton became subject to a federal law known as the Hatch Act, which prohibits federal employees from personally soliciting or accepting political contributions. The Hatch Act allows others to keep raising money on Clinton's behalf, without her direct involvement. This week, longtime Clinton ally James Carville, a CNN contributor, sent a fundraising e-mail to Democrats on behalf of Clinton's campaign, requesting contributions of as little as $5 in exchange for a chance to win one of several prizes, including spending a day with former President Bill Clinton. "I won't spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary," Carville e-mailed. "I know what she means to you, and I'm sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations." It's unclear whether the campaign will use the $2.6 million in the bank to clear its $2.3 million in debts in the short term. Continued fundraising indicates that it will not. Additional operating expenses and other outlays could emerge. Any extra money from the campaign could be donated to political causes or returned to donors. Clinton's campaign reported raising $938,000 in contributions in the first three months of 2009. In addition to tapping traditional fundraising, the campaign also generated money by selling or renting various campaign assets to other organizations. It received $2.6 million from Clinton's "Friends of Hillary" U.S. Senate campaign committee for the sale of unspecified assets and an additional $2.2 million from renting out its lists of campaign supporters. Organizations that have rented Clinton's lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee of then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Those organizations each paid $274,297. Clinton's political action committee, HillPAC, rented the lists for $822,492. Among the Democratic candidates who have rented Clinton's campaign lists are Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former Clinton campaign Chairman Terry McAuliffe; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton's seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who hopes to succeed Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

Clinton’s campaign committee reported $2.3 million in debt at the end of March. On a day when most Americans were focused on filing their federal income taxes, the committee submitted finance documents to the Federal Election Commission showing $2.3 million in debts, compared with $2.6 million in the bank.

The nation’s top diplomat has been steadily reducing unpaid campaign bills since suspending her White House bid in June 2008, when her debt peaked at $25.2 million. That total included $12 million owed to vendors, as well as $13.2 million she had loaned her campaign from personal funds.

Clinton’s campaign was unable to repay that personal loan by the time the Democratic National Convention convened in Denver, Colorado, last August—the deadline set by the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. As a result, the former New York senator was required to forgive the entire loan amount.

Her campaign owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors at the end of November, $5.9 million to five creditors at the end of December, and now $2.3 million to just one creditor at the end of March. That creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a political consulting and polling firm that advised Clinton during her presidential campaign.

The firm’s president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton’s senior campaign strategist until stepping down last April amid revelations that he had lobbied on behalf of Colombia in support of a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement that Clinton opposed. Penn remained involved with the campaign.

Earlier this year, Clinton and her supporters moved quickly to pay down as much of the debt as possible before she was confirmed and sworn in as the nation’s 67th secretary of state on January 21. As of that date, Clinton became subject to the Hatch Act, a federal law that prohibits federal employees from personally soliciting or accepting political contributions.

The Hatch Act permits others to continue raising money on Clinton’s behalf, provided she is not directly involved.

This week, longtime Clinton ally James Carville, a CNN contributor, sent a fundraising e-mail to Democrats on behalf of Clinton’s campaign. He requested contributions of as little as $5 in exchange for a chance to win one of several prizes, including spending a day with former President Bill Clinton.

“I won’t spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary,” Carville wrote. “I know what she means to you, and I’m sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations.”

It remains unclear whether the campaign will use the $2.6 million it has in the bank to eliminate its $2.3 million in debt in the near term. Continued fundraising suggests that it will not. Additional operating expenses and other outlays could also arise. Any surplus campaign funds could be donated to political causes or returned to donors.

Clinton’s campaign reported raising $938,000 in contributions during the first three months of 2009. In addition to traditional fundraising, the campaign generated revenue by selling or renting various campaign assets to other organizations.

It received $2.6 million from Clinton’s “Friends of Hillary” U.S. Senate campaign committee for the sale of unspecified assets, as well as an additional $2.2 million from renting its lists of campaign supporters.

Organizations that rented Clinton’s lists include the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee of then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Each of those organizations paid $274,297. Clinton’s political action committee, HillPAC, rented the lists for $822,492.

Among the Democratic candidates who rented Clinton’s campaign lists are Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former Clinton campaign chairman Terry McAuliffe; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to fill Clinton’s Senate seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who is seeking to succeed Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

At the end of March, Clinton’s campaign committee reported $2.3 million in debt. While many Americans were focused on submitting their federal income tax returns, the committee filed financial reports with the Federal Election Commission showing $2.3 million owed and $2.6 million on hand.

Clinton, the country’s chief diplomat, has been gradually reducing unpaid campaign expenses since she ended her presidential campaign in June 2008. At that time, her debt had reached a high of $25.2 million. That figure included $12 million owed to vendors and $13.2 million that Clinton had personally lent to her campaign.

Her campaign did not repay that personal loan before the Democratic National Convention opened in Denver, Colorado, the previous August. That was the deadline set under the 2002 McCain-Feingold campaign finance law. As a result, the former senator from New York had to forgive the full loan.

The campaign’s debt has fallen steadily. It owed $6.4 million to 16 creditors at the end of November, $5.9 million to five creditors at the end of December, and, by the end of March, $2.3 million to a single creditor.

That remaining creditor is Penn, Schoen & Berland, a polling and political consulting company that worked for Clinton during her presidential campaign. The firm’s president, Mark Penn, served as Clinton’s chief campaign strategist until he resigned the previous April after disclosures that he had lobbied for Colombia in support of a U.S.-Colombia trade agreement that Clinton opposed. Penn continued to have a role in the campaign afterward.

Earlier in the year, Clinton and her backers worked quickly to retire as much of the debt as they could before she was confirmed and sworn in as the 67th U.S. secretary of state on January 21. Once she took office, Clinton became covered by the Hatch Act, a federal law that bars federal employees from personally asking for or receiving political donations.

The Hatch Act does permit others to continue raising funds for Clinton, as long as she is not directly involved.

This week, James Carville, a longtime Clinton supporter and CNN contributor, sent a fundraising e-mail to Democrats for Clinton’s campaign. He asked for donations as small as $5, offering contributors a chance to win several prizes, including spending a day with former President Bill Clinton.

“I won’t spend a lot of time trying to convince you to help Hillary,” Carville wrote in the e-mail. “I know what she means to you, and I’m sure you know how important it is for her to have her campaign pay off all its obligations.”

It is not certain whether the campaign will soon use its $2.6 million in available funds to pay off the $2.3 million still owed. The fact that fundraising is continuing suggests it may not do so immediately. More operating costs or other expenses could still arise.

Any money left over from the campaign could be given to political causes or refunded to contributors.

Clinton’s campaign said it raised $938,000 in donations during the first quarter of 2009. Beyond regular fundraising, the campaign also brought in revenue by selling or leasing different campaign assets to other groups.

It received $2.6 million from Clinton’s “Friends of Hillary” U.S. Senate campaign committee for the sale of unidentified assets. It also collected another $2.2 million by renting out its lists of campaign supporters.

Groups that rented Clinton’s lists included the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the inaugural committee of then-President-elect Barack Obama, and the William Jefferson Clinton Foundation. Each of those organizations paid $274,297.

Clinton’s political action committee, HillPAC, paid $822,492 to rent the lists.

Democratic candidates who have rented Clinton’s campaign lists include Arkansas Sen. Blanche Lincoln; Terry McAuliffe, the Virginia gubernatorial candidate and former chairman of Clinton’s presidential campaign; New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, who was appointed to take Clinton’s Senate seat; and New York congressional candidate Scott Murphy, who is seeking to replace Gillibrand in the U.S. House.

**Clinton’s 2008 campaign reports more cash than debt in latest FEC filing**

*By CNN-style report*

Hillary Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign committee has crossed a notable financial milestone: It now reports more money in the bank than outstanding debt, according to its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission.

The committee, **Hillary Clinton for President**, still exists years after Clinton ended her first White House bid largely because of debts left over from the bruising Democratic primary fight against Barack Obama. The newest report shows the campaign with **more cash on hand than remaining liabilities**, a sign that the long-running debt-retirement effort is nearing its end.

Most of the remaining debt is tied to vendors from the 2008 race, including money owed to **Penn, Schoen & Berland**, the polling and consulting firm associated with longtime Clinton adviser **Mark Penn**, who served as the campaign’s chief strategist during much of the primary contest. Penn’s firm was among the campaign’s largest creditors after Clinton suspended her campaign.

The committee’s ability to retire the debt was complicated during Clinton’s tenure as secretary of state. Under federal ethics rules, including restrictions associated with the **Hatch Act**, Clinton was limited in her ability to engage in political fundraising while serving in the Obama administration. Those limits meant the committee had to rely on others to help raise money and on nontraditional revenue streams.

One of those revenue sources has been **list rentals**. The campaign committee has continued to earn money by renting its donor and supporter lists to other political committees and organizations — a common practice for campaigns with valuable fundraising lists. Those rentals helped bring in funds even as Clinton herself was largely sidelined from direct political fundraising while in office.

Clinton’s 2008 campaign ended with millions of dollars in unpaid bills, including substantial sums owed to consultants and vendors, as well as money Clinton personally loaned her campaign. Over time, the committee has steadily reduced those obligations through contributions, transfers and list-rental income.

The latest filing does not mean the committee is fully closed, but it marks a significant step toward winding down one of the most expensive primary campaigns in Democratic Party history.

**WASHINGTON —** Hillary Rodham Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign, long over but not fully paid for, continued to draw money in early 2009 as supporters worked to erase the remaining debt from her losing Democratic primary bid, newly filed Federal Election Commission reports show.

Clinton, now secretary of state, entered the year with millions still owed to vendors and consultants from her bruising contest against President Barack Obama. FEC filings from the first quarter of 2009 show her campaign committee, Friends of Hillary, raised roughly **$5.6 million** from January through March, allowing it to sharply reduce its outstanding obligations.

The committee reported debt of about **$6.4 million** at the start of the year and cut that figure to roughly **$2.3 million** by the end of March, according to the filings. The campaign also reported several million dollars in remaining cash on hand, putting Clinton within reach of closing the books on one of the most expensive primary campaigns in American history.

Clinton’s campaign once carried debts totaling more than $20 million, including money she lent the effort herself during the 2008 primaries. Much of the remaining debt in early 2009 was owed to campaign vendors, consultants and service providers. Her personal loans were no longer the chief issue; the campaign’s immediate priority was paying outside creditors.

Because Clinton joined Obama’s Cabinet in January, her fundraising role has been sharply limited. Federal ethics rules and administration guidelines restrict Cabinet officials from personally soliciting political contributions. Aides have said Clinton has not been asking donors for money since becoming secretary of state, leaving debt-retirement efforts to campaign supporters and fundraisers.

The continuing fundraising nonetheless underscored the unusual political position Clinton occupied in early 2009: serving as the nation’s chief diplomat while a campaign committee bearing her name remained active and accepting contributions. Republicans and government watchdogs have raised questions about the appearance of donors contributing to a fund tied to a sitting secretary of state, particularly given the State Department’s broad international portfolio.

Clinton allies say the fundraising is legal, routine and narrowly focused on retiring old campaign bills. Under federal law, candidates may continue raising money after an election to pay down campaign debt, subject to contribution limits and disclosure requirements.

The filings show that many donors who had backed Clinton during the 2008 race continued to contribute after Obama took office. The debt-retirement push also benefited from the extensive donor network Clinton built during her presidential campaign and from the continued political activity of former President Bill Clinton and other longtime supporters.

Clinton’s 2008 campaign was among the most formidable ever mounted by a losing primary candidate. She won nearly 18 million votes and carried major states including California, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas, but Obama secured the Democratic nomination after a prolonged delegate fight. After conceding in June 2008, Clinton campaigned actively for Obama and was later nominated to lead the State Department.

The first-quarter FEC numbers suggested that the financial aftermath of the campaign was finally nearing an end. If fundraising continued at the same pace, Clinton’s committee appeared positioned to retire the remaining debt later in 2009, allowing the secretary of state to fully close a costly chapter from her presidential bid.

**Clinton 2008 campaign debt shrank rapidly through fundraising, write-offs and asset sales**

*CNN-style report*

Hillary Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign, once burdened by more than $25 million in debt after her bruising Democratic primary fight with Barack Obama, had reduced that obligation to about $2.3 million by the end of March 2009, according to federal campaign finance filings.

The dramatic decline was the result of several factors: Clinton’s decision to absorb much of the money she had personally loaned the campaign, aggressive post-primary debt-retirement fundraising, payments to major vendors and consultants, and the sale of leftover campaign assets.

By the time Clinton ended her presidential bid in June 2008, her campaign was carrying roughly **$25.2 million in debt**, a figure that included both unpaid bills to vendors and loans Clinton had made to keep the campaign operating during the final months of the nomination battle.

A large share of that total was owed not to outside vendors, but to Clinton herself. She had loaned her campaign more than $13 million during the primary race. Under federal election rules and political realities, recovering all of that money became increasingly unlikely once the campaign ended. Clinton ultimately wrote off most of her personal loans, a move that sharply reduced the campaign’s reported debt burden.

The remaining debt consisted largely of unpaid obligations to consultants, pollsters, media firms, printers, travel vendors and other companies that had provided services during the campaign.

Among the campaign’s best-known creditors was **Penn, Schoen & Berland Associates**, the polling and consulting firm associated with Mark Penn, Clinton’s former chief strategist. The firm was one of several vendors owed substantial sums after the primary. Other creditors included media-production and direct-mail firms, communications consultants, event vendors, and companies that handled travel, technology, printing and logistical work for the national campaign.

After Clinton suspended her campaign and endorsed Obama, her political operation continued to raise money specifically to retire debt. Supporters who had not already given the legal maximum for the primary election were solicited for contributions. Clinton also benefited from party unity efforts after the primary, including help from Democratic donors eager to close the books on the nominating contest and move toward the general election.

Those fundraising efforts continued into 2009, even after Clinton had been nominated and confirmed as secretary of state in the Obama administration. Because she could no longer personally take part in political fundraising once she joined the administration, her campaign committee relied on remaining staff, surrogates and existing donor networks to collect outstanding contributions for debt retirement.

Federal Election Commission reports showed the campaign bringing in millions of dollars after the race ended. Contributions from donors were used to pay down vendors who had been waiting months for full payment.

The committee also raised money through the sale of remaining campaign assets. Like many large national campaigns, Clinton’s operation had accumulated office equipment, computers, furniture, lists, and other assets during the primary. After the campaign shut down its field and headquarters operations, those items could be sold, with proceeds used to pay outstanding bills. Campaign filings reflected asset sales as part of the committee’s effort to reduce its liabilities.

By March 31, 2009, Clinton’s campaign reported only about **$2.3 million in remaining debt**, a fraction of what it had owed less than a year earlier.

The reduction underscored how much of the original debt figure depended on Clinton’s own loans. Once those were largely written off, the campaign’s remaining challenge was to satisfy outside creditors. Continued fundraising and liquidation of campaign property allowed the committee to pay down most of those obligations.

The debt retirement also carried political significance. Clinton had ended the 2008 primary as the runner-up to Obama, but she remained one of the Democratic Party’s most influential figures. Paying vendors and closing out campaign obligations helped resolve one of the lingering financial issues from the long and costly primary contest.

By early 2009, with Clinton serving as secretary of state and Obama in the White House, the campaign’s once-massive debt had been reduced to a manageable final balance.

WASHINGTON — Hillary Rodham Clinton’s move from presidential candidate to secretary of state has left her 2008 campaign facing an unusual financial problem: how to retire lingering debt when the candidate herself is barred from raising money.

In the days before Clinton’s Senate confirmation, longtime ally James Carville appealed to supporters in a fundraising e-mail, urging them to help close the books on her presidential bid while she was still legally able to solicit contributions. The message underscored the shrinking window available to Clinton’s political operation as she prepared to join President Barack Obama’s Cabinet.

Once confirmed as secretary of state, Clinton became subject to Hatch Act restrictions that prohibit federal employees from engaging in many forms of partisan political activity, including personally soliciting campaign contributions. That means Clinton cannot headline fundraisers, sign fundraising appeals or ask donors to help pay off her campaign debt.

Her campaign committee, however, may continue to raise money without her direct involvement. Aides and supporters can solicit contributions, and the committee can use other means to bring in revenue. One such method has been renting access to Clinton’s extensive lists of supporters — names compiled during her hard-fought Democratic primary campaign against Obama.

Those lists are valuable political assets. Campaigns, party committees and advocacy groups often pay to rent donor or supporter lists to seek new contributors or activists. Clinton’s campaign has used list rentals as a way to generate income while complying with legal limits on her own political role.

Clinton ended the 2008 race with millions of dollars in unpaid bills and personal loans to her campaign. Although some of the debt was gradually reduced after she suspended her candidacy and endorsed Obama, the remaining obligations followed her into the transition period.

The situation highlights the complications that can arise when a former presidential candidate joins the government before fully winding down a campaign operation. Clinton’s political allies can continue the work of retiring the debt, but the new secretary of state must remain at arm’s length from the fundraising effort.
